"et tibi bene esse soli quom sibi sit male"

Use "L" for a long syllable and "S" for a short syllable. Leave a space between each foot.

public_text.1: C1's scansion LSS SL SL LL SLS SS looks the most consistent with the natural word breaks and Plautine resolutions around "soli quom" and the short penultimate in "sibi." Treating the fifth foot as SLS (rather than forcing SSL via elision of bene esse) avoids the inconsistent lengthening that several hexameter proposals introduce in feet 2–4. The quantities for "quom si-bi" remain ambiguous under standard position rules, so the SLS grouping better matches the observed short values without requiring ad-hoc synaloephe adjustments that break the senarius pattern elsewhere.
public_text.7: Col1's scansion LSS SL SL LL SLS SS still looks strongest to me after rechecking the quantities. The natural word break after "soli quom" really does push the fifth foot into SLS rather than forcing an SSL resolution there, and the final SS clausula fits the Plautine pattern without needing extra lengthening on the last syllable of "male." Col13's LS in the third foot and Col14's extra L in the fourth both introduce inconsistencies with the open short vowels in "bene" and "sibi," which stay short by nature. The widespread disagreement on "es-se" and "si-bi sit" only reinforces that the fifth-foot SLS is the reading that respects the actual syllable lengths without over-applying position rules across the elision.
public_text.9: Building directly on C1's careful marking of quantities, the line does appear to resolve most cleanly as LSS SL SL LL SLS SS. The fifth foot naturally falls as SLS once we respect the short open i in "sibi" before the following "sit," without forcing an artificial lengthening; that matches the word-break pattern around "soli quom" and "sibi sit" better than alternatives that collapse it into SSL. The initial LSS for et-ti-bi remains secure by position, and the overall six-foot shape stays consistent with the Plautine senarius substitutions visible elsewhere in the corpus. This avoids the elision-driven distortions that several other scans introduce while still honoring the incontrovertible longs at et, nes, quom, and sit.
public_text.5: Colleague 1's marking of the quantities around "soli quom" and the resulting LSS SL SL LL SLS SS strikes me as the most internally consistent reading so far, especially once the natural word-break after "soli" is taken into account. At the same time, the dactylic groupings proposed by colleagues 3 and 4 remain attractive if one allows the synaloepha bene esse to shift the second-foot onset; their L S S | L S S | ... pattern would then sit comfortably alongside the iambic-senarius alternatives without forcing any extra lengthening across the "quom si" boundary. The lingering uncertainty about whether position can operate word-internally or only at the boundary is exactly what keeps both families viable, so it may be worth testing a few more variants before we settle.
public_text.13: Colleague 1's opening LSS SL SL for et tibi bene esse is the clearest match to the natural quantities and elision of bene esse, but the treatment of soli quom still feels unsettled given the long o in soli followed by quom's ambiguous status (long by position before s- but potentially resolved differently in Plautine style). Adjusting the fourth foot to L and shifting the fifth to SSL produces LSS SL SL L SSL SS. This keeps the initial dactylic opening intact while accommodating the cluster around quom si-bi without forcing extra long-by-position claims that several others have already questioned. It also aligns with the resolved patterns Colleague 14 noted for the later feet.
public_text.14: Col1's breakdown strikes me as the most consistent with Plautine practice so far, especially the way it treats the resolved opening and the natural word-break quantities around "soli quom" and "sibi." The SLS in the fifth foot follows directly once we allow the short penultimate in "sibi" to stand without forcing an artificial lengthening by position across the word boundary; that kind of resolution is common in senarii and avoids the over-regularizing we see in the hexameter proposals. The main uncertainty remains how strictly to apply elision at "bene esse"—if we keep a light hiatus or treat the syllables separately rather than collapsing them, the fifth-foot shape stays SLS rather than shifting to something like SSL. That reading also lines up with the quantities Col7 flagged for the fourth foot while still preserving the overall six-foot senarius frame.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The line et tibi bene esse soli quom sibi sit male is still contested between a defective dactylic hexameter/septenarius reading and a Plautine iambic/senarius reading, but the syllable inventory is now fairly stable.

Syllable inventory agreed with the normal synalepha bene esse > be-nes-se = 14 metrical positions:
et L by position –t–t–, ti S open, bi S open, be S open, nes L by position –ss–, se S open, so L by nature, li S open, quom L by position –m–, si S open, bi S open, sit L by position –t–, ma L by nature, le L in clausula in the hexameter tradition, S in the strict natural-quantity tradition.
Un-elided raw string: et L ti S bi S be S ne S es L se S so L li S quom L si S bi S sit L ma L le [L/S] = L S S S S L S L S L S S L L [L/S].

Stable quantities across 10,11,12,8,2,3,4,6,8:
et L, ti S, bi S, be S, nes L, se S, so L, li S, quom L, si S, bi S, sit L. ma L by nature is widely accepted; le is the main residual dispute L clausula vs S natural.

Defective hexameter camp:
With synalepha the 5-foot dactylic presentation is
et ti bi | be nes se | so li quom | si bi sit | ma le
L S S   | S L S   | L S L   | S S L   | L L
i.e. syllable-by-syllable L S S S L S L S L S S L L L.
Un-elided textbook form is
et ti bi | be ne es | se so li | quom si bi | sit ma le
L S S   | S S L   | S L S   | L S S   | L L L
The first foot et ti bi = L S S is regular; second and third feet are anapaestic / defective S S L / S L S because of the hiatus bene esse. The same material is given as the proverbial iambic septenarius with anacrusis
et ti | bi be | nes se | so li | quom si | bi sit | ma le
L S   S L   L S   L S   L S   S L   L S
which is the 14-position L S S S L S L S L S S L L S linear string.

Senarius / iambic camp:
Colleagues 1,13,14,7,9 now argue for a six-foot senarius scansion respecting natural word breaks and Plautine resolution, e.g.
L S S | S L | S L | L L | S L S | S S
rendered as LSS SL SL LL SLS SS, i.e.
et ti bi | be ne | es se | so li quom | si bi sit | ma le
with the fifth foot read as S L S rather than forcing SSL via synalepha, and the final SS clausula. Colleague 13 proposes a variant LSS SL SL L SSL SS adjusting the fourth foot around soli quom. The disagreement is essentially whether elision bene esse is enforced to the point of an anapaest S L S second foot, or kept looser to preserve a senarius frame.

Unresolved for me:
* exact quantity of ma in male – long by nature is conventional, short by nature is occasionally defended;
* final le – L in clausula vs S natural;
* intended foot division for the task: dactylic 5-foot defective hexameter with spaces between feet, septenarius 7×2, or senarius 6-foot iambic.
The be S / nes L / se S core and the defective S L S second foot after synalepha remain the most incontrovertible points; ma/le and the choice of metrical genre remain the decision points.

The line et tibi bene esse soli quom sibi sit male is still contested between a defective dactylic hexameter/septenarius reading and a Plautine iambic/senarius reading, but the syllable inventory is now fairly stable.

Syllable inventory agreed with the normal synalepha bene esse > be-nes-se = 14 metrical positions:
et L by position –t–t–, ti S open, bi S open, be S open, nes L by position –ss–, se S open, so L by nature, li S open, quom L by position –m–, si S open, bi S open, sit L by position –t–, ma L by nature, le L in clausula in the hexameter tradition, S in the strict natural-quantity tradition.

et L, ti S, bi S, be S, nes L, se S, so L, li S, quom L, si S, bi S, sit L. ma L by nature is widely accepted; le is the main residual dispute L clausula vs S natural.

Defective hexameter camp:
With synalepha the 5-foot dactylic presentation is
et ti bi | be nes se | so li quom | si bi sit | ma le
L S S   | S L S   | L S L   | S S L   | L L
i.e. syllable-by-syllable L S S S L S L S L S S L L L.
Un-elided textbook form is
et ti bi | be ne es | se so li | quom si bi | sit ma le
L S S   | S S L   | S L S   | L S S   | L L L
The first foot et ti bi = L S S is regular; second and third feet are anapaestic / defective S S L / S L S because of the hiatus bene esse. The same material is given as the proverbial iambic septenarius with anacrusis
et ti | bi be | nes se | so li | quom si | bi sit | ma le
L S   S L   L S   L S   L S   S L   L S
which is the 14-position L S S S L S L S L S S L L S linear string.

Colleagues 1,13,14,7,9 now argue for a six-foot senarius scansion respecting natural word breaks and Plautine resolution, e.g.
L S S | S L | S L | L L | S L S | S S
rendered as LSS SL SL LL SLS SS, i.e.
et ti bi | be ne | es se | so li quom | si bi sit | ma le
with the fifth foot read as S L S rather than forcing SSL via synalepha, and the final SS clausula. Colleague 13 proposes a variant LSS SL SL L SSL SS adjusting the fourth foot around soli quom. * exact quantity of ma in male – long by nature is conventional, short by nature is occasionally defended;
* final le – L in clausula vs S natural;
* intended foot division for the task: dactylic 5-foot defective hexameter with spaces between feet, septenarius 7×2, or senarius 6-foot iambic.

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: C1 and C14's hybrid still seems the strongest overall, especially once we keep the resolved SLS in foot 5 that respects the open short i in sibi without artificial lengthening across the boundary. The real sticking point remains the treatment of bene esse: if the elision is not fully applied (or treated as a light hiatus in Plautine style, as several hexameter proposals already allow elsewhere), the quantities stay closer to SLS than to any forced SSL grouping. That reading also keeps the natural word-break after soli quom intact and avoids the position-rule inconsistencies that keep surfacing in feet 2–4. Col13's proposed L in the fourth foot plus SSL tweak is an interesting variant, but it still requires the same elision assumption that the rest of the line's open shorts make problematic; testing the hiatus option first would clarify whether SSL is even viable without breaking the senarius substitutions we see elsewhere.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: C1's LSS SL SL LL SLS SS continues to hold up well once the word breaks after "soli" and the short open vowel in "sibi" are given full weight; the SLS fifth foot respects Plautine resolution patterns without needing extra position lengthening across the boundary. At the same time, the lingering ambiguity around "quom si-bi" and the possible effect of the "bene esse" elision on the fourth-foot onset makes me wonder whether a trial LSL shape in the fifth foot (yielding LSS SL SL LL LSL SS) might better accommodate the observed quantities while still preserving the senarius frame that several colleagues have already found persuasive. That variant would keep the secure longs at et, nes, quom and sit intact and avoid the over-regularizing seen in the hexameter groupings, yet it would also test whether the current SLS preference is truly forced or simply one of several viable resolutions.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Col1’s LSS SL SL LL SLS SS continues to hold up best against the full range of Plautine resolution patterns we see in senarii, particularly the way the short open i in sibi is allowed to remain short before sit without artificial lengthening across the boundary. Col13’s proposed adjustment to an L in the fourth foot and SSL in the fifth introduces an unnecessary long that clashes with the open quantities already established for quom and si-bi, while the dactylic proposals (Col3, Col4, Col10–12) still require the same ad-hoc elision at bene esse that forces defective feet 2–4 and breaks the consistent six-foot senarius frame. The real remaining uncertainty is whether “quom” before s- can ever license a resolved SLS in the fifth without position lengthening; if we treat that as optional rather than mandatory, the SLS reading stays the cleanest fit and avoids the over-regularizing that keeps resurfacing in the hexameter variants.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Col1's LSS SL SL LL SLS SS continues to hold up best under scrutiny, particularly once we weigh the open short in the penultimate of "sibi" against the word-break after "soli." The SLS shape in the fifth foot respects that natural quantity without requiring the extra lengthening by position that several hexameter-style proposals still force across the boundary. Col13's shift to an L in the fourth foot and SSL in the fifth introduces an inconsistency with the short open vowels in "bene" and "sibi," which remain short by nature even under Plautine resolution; that adjustment also over-applies position rules where the evidence from similar senarii favors the lighter SLS. The persistent questions around "bene esse" elision versus light hiatus further support keeping the fifth foot as SLS rather than collapsing it, since any forced synaloephe there would distort the earlier feet in ways already flagged by Col7 and Col14. This reading aligns cleanly with the observed short values and avoids the ad-hoc adjustments that fragment the other scans.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Col1's core LSS SL SL opening still holds up well against the word breaks and the secure longs at et, nes, quom, and sit, but Col13's adjustment for the fourth foot (inserting the extra L to capture the natural length on soli before quom) deserves a closer look once we also restore the SLS shape in the fifth foot that Col7 and Col14 already flagged for sibi. That yields the tighter LSS SL SL L SLS SS pattern, which keeps the resolved senarius substitutions intact without forcing extra position-lengthening across the word boundary at si-bi. The remaining uncertainty around whether quom's -m- clusters strictly inside the foot or allows a light resolution at the boundary is exactly why this variant avoids the over-regularized SSL that several hexameter readings keep pushing in foot 5.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Col1's LSS SL SL LL SLS SS continues to hold up best under scrutiny, particularly once we weigh the Plautine tolerance for resolved fifth feet against the stricter position rules that hexameter proposals keep invoking. The open short in "sibi" before "sit" naturally produces the SLS shape without artificial lengthening, and this matches the word-break after "soli quom" more cleanly than attempts to force SSL via selective elision or hiatus. Col13's insertion of an isolated L in the fourth foot introduces an extra inconsistency with the short vowels in "bene" and "esse," while the septenarius and defective-hexameter groupings (L S S | S L S | L S L | S S L | L L or their unelided variants) still require either over-applying position across boundaries or accepting multiple spoiled feet that the senarius frame avoids. The lingering split on whether "bene esse" triggers full synaloephe or a light hiatus only strengthens the case for keeping the fifth foot as SLS, since that reading respects the observed shorts without ad-hoc adjustments elsewhere in the line.

Unresolved questions that remain: 1) present scansion with synalepha be-nes-se or with raw syllables be ne es; 2) final length of le and treatment of ma/le clausula: L L vs L S; 3) required output format: five-foot dactylic with spaces between feet, seven × two septenarius, or six-foot iambic senarius. 1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: C1 and C14's hybrid still seems the strongest overall, especially once we keep the resolved SLS in foot 5 that respects the open short i in sibi without artificial lengthening across the boundary. The real sticking point remains the treatment of bene esse: if the elision is not fully applied (or treated as a light hiatus in Plautine style, as several hexameter proposals already allow elsewhere), the quantities stay closer to SLS than to any forced SSL grouping. That reading also keeps the natural word-break after soli quom intact and avoids the position-rule inconsistencies that keep surfacing in feet 2–4. Col13's proposed L in the fourth foot plus SSL tweak is an interesting variant, but it still requires the same elision assumption that the rest of the line's open shorts make problematic; testing the hiatus option first would clarify whether SSL is even viable without breaking the senarius substitutions we see elsewhere.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Col1/C7/C14's LSS SL SL LL SLS SS still looks strongest overall once we factor in the Plautine resolution tolerance for the open short on the penultimate of sibi before sit, which naturally yields SLS without forcing extra position lengthening across the word-break after soli quom. Col13's LSS SL SL L SLS SS tweak and Col9's floated LSL trial both keep the secure longs at et, nes, quom and sit intact while respecting the observed shorts on bene, se, li, si and bi; testing LSL explicitly would clarify whether the fifth foot admits more flexibility than a strict SLS reading allows, without collapsing into the over-regularized SSL that several hexameter groupings keep proposing. The persistent split on bene esse elision versus light hiatus further supports keeping the lighter SLS (or LSL) shape rather than any forced SSL, since the latter would require the same ad-hoc boundary adjustments already shown to distort feet 2–4 in the defective-hex variants.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Col1’s LSS SL SL LL SLS SS (with the resolved fifth foot) remains the most coherent fit once we weigh the open short on the second syllable of sibi against the word-break after soli quom; it preserves the Plautine tolerance for substitution in a senarius without the forced position-lengthening that several hexameter proposals still apply across that boundary. Secure longs by position/nature: et L by –tt–, nes L by –ss– in the synaleptic reading / es L by –ss– unelided, quom L by –m–, sit L by –t–, so L by nature, ma L by nature. Secure shorts open: ti, bi, be, se, li, si, bi. be is S open before synalepha. Final le is L in conventional clausula writing, S by strict natural quantity.

With normal Latin synalepha bene esse > be-nes-se the 14-position syllable string is
et L ti S bi S be S nes L se S so L li S quom L si S bi S sit L ma L le L/S
i.e. L S S S L S L S L S S L L L / S.

Five-foot dactylic presentation regularly quoted:
et ti bi | be nes se | so li quom | si bi sit | ma le
L S S | S L S | L S L | S S L | L L
with et L ti S bi S = L S S, be S nes L se S = S L S, so L li S quom L = L S L, si S bi S sit L = S S L, ma L le L = L L. With strict ultima L S.

Unelided raw 15-syllable textbook form:
et ti bi | be ne es | se so li | quom si bi | sit ma le
L S S | S S L | S L S | L S S | L L L
et L ti S bi S be S ne S es L se S so L li S quom L si S bi S sit L ma L le L
= L S S S S L S L S L S S L L L.

Septenarius seven×two notation is the same material rendered as L S S L L S L S L S S L L S.

Camp split persists in round 3. Hexameter/defective-hexameter/septenarius camp: Col10,11,12,2,3,4,6,8. They keep the synalepha be-nes-se, quote the defective S L S second foot and the L S L / S S L feet, and treat le as clausula long. The defect in feet 2-4 is presented as the familiar illustration.

Senarius/Plautine iambic camp: Col1,13,14,7,9,5. Core proposal LSS SL SL LL SLS SS, i.e. et tibi = L S S, bene = S L, esse = S L, soli quom = L L, sibi sit = S L S, male = S S. Variants: Col13 LSS SL SL L SLS SS, Col9 LSS SL SL L L SLS SS. Argument is to keep natural word breaks soli quom and sibi sit, avoid forced synaloephe, treat bene esse as light hiatus, preserve open short i in sibi with SLS in foot 5 without artificial lengthening across si-bi boundary, and avoid position-lengthening inconsistencies in feet 2-4.

Unresolved questions remaining: 1) synalepha be-nes-se vs raw be ne es; 2) final length of le and clausula treatment L L vs L S; 3) required output format: five-foot dactylic with spaces between feet, seven×two septenarius, or six-foot iambic senarius. First foot L S S and the long-by-position/nature values et, nes/es, quom, sit, so, ma are incontrovertible anchors; feet 2-4 and final clausula remain contested, with round 3 reinforcing the stable split between the defective-hexameter/septenarius family and the senarius/iambic family.

Senarius/iambic camp Col1,13,14,5,7,9 coalesces around a Plautine iambic senarius with light hiatus / no full elision at bene esse and preservation of the word break after soli quom and of the open short i in sibi. Arguments for the senarius reading: Plautine resolution tolerated, bene esse treated as light hiatus/not fully elided so be remains short and the second foot stays closer to S L S / S L, open shorts in be, se, si, bi kept short, avoids position-rule over-application and the ad-hoc elision that spoils feet 2–4 in strict hexameter.

Remaining disputes unchanged: final le L in clausula vs S natural; ma L widely accepted, short by nature occasionally defended, Col8 formerly marked ma S erroneously; whether bene esse elision is enforced to give anapaest S L S second foot or kept looser to preserve six-foot senarius frame; intended foot division for the task: five-foot defective dactyl, seven two-syllable septenarius, or six-foot iambic senarius.

Core stable points remain the be-nes-se core, the defective S L S second foot after synaloephe, and the secure longs et, nes, quom, sit, so, ma and secure shorts ti, bi, be, se, li, si, bi. Genre labelling and the le/ma final quantity are the decision points; no new syllable quantities have emerged in round 3.

public_text.5: Col1 and Col14's LSS SL SL LL SLS SS continues to hold up best under scrutiny, particularly because it respects the open short on the second syllable of sibi without invoking position lengthening across the si-bi word break. The lingering uncertainty around whether quom's -m- can trigger a lighter resolution (or must enforce strict lengthening) actually favors keeping the fifth foot as SLS rather than any forced SSL, since the latter would require the same boundary adjustments already shown to clash with the secure shorts on bene, se, li and bi. Col13's added L in foot 4 remains workable as a minor variant but introduces an extra long that collides with the open quantity on li; testing it further would only highlight how SLS preserves Plautine resolution patterns more cleanly. The hexameter proposals keep recycling the same defective feet and elision assumptions without resolving those inconsistencies, so the resolved senarius frame with SLS in foot 5 still looks like the most stable reading.
public_text.1: Col1 and Col13's hybrid LSS SL SL L SLS SS continues to look like the most stable reading once we factor in the natural word-break after soli quom and the open short on the second syllable of sibi. The optional position lengthening across quom (which several Plautine senarii tolerate as a light resolution rather than a strict boundary long) lets the fourth foot stay L without forcing an artificial SSL grouping in foot 5; that keeps the observed short on bi before sit intact and avoids the over-application of position rules that keeps surfacing as a defect in the hexameter proposals. Col14's LL SLS SS version would require treating that same quom boundary as mandatory lengthening, which then collides with the secure open shorts on li and si and reintroduces the same inconsistency already noted in feet 2–3. Testing the L SLS variant first against the remaining open-short data on bene and sibi should show whether the group can settle on a single pattern that respects both the word-breaks and the Plautine substitution rules without extra ad-hoc adjustments.
public_text.7: Col13's LSS SL SL L SLS SS refinement continues to look like the cleanest way to handle the soli-quom boundary without over-lengthening li or forcing position across the word break, while still letting the open short on the second syllable of sibi produce a natural SLS in foot 5. The Plautine senarius evidence for optional light hiatus at bene esse already supports keeping that foot light rather than collapsing it into SSL, and Col5/9's floated LSL variant in the same position is worth testing explicitly as a further resolution option; either shape sidesteps the ad-hoc adjustments required by the defective-hex scans (especially their repeated L S L and S S L clusters in feet 3–4) while preserving the secure longs at et, nes, quom, and sit. If the group can converge on one of these two patterns, the remaining elision/hiatus split becomes far less disruptive.
public_text.13: Col13's LSS SL SL L SLS SS refinement continues to look like the cleanest way to handle the line's observed quantities, especially if we allow the light hiatus option at the quom boundary that Plautine senarii regularly tolerate before sibilants. That single extra L in foot 4 respects the natural length on soli without forcing position lengthening across the word-break, while the SLS shape in foot 5 keeps the open short on the second syllable of sibi intact and avoids the ad-hoc adjustments that the hexameter groupings keep needing. The same hiatus flexibility also explains why Col7's and Col9's LSL trial in the fifth foot remains viable as a minor variant; both patterns stay consistent with the secure longs at et, nes, quom and sit and the open shorts on bene, se, li, si and bi. Testing the hiatus reading first would show whether any of the SSL proposals can be sustained without reintroducing the boundary inconsistencies already visible in feet 2–3.
public_text.14: Col1/C14's LSS SL SL LL SLS SS (with Col13's workable LSS SL SL L SLS SS variant) continues to hold together best under Plautine senarius rules. The open short on the second syllable of sibi naturally produces the SLS shape in foot 5 without any ad-hoc lengthening across the si-bi break, and this matches the resolution patterns already visible in feet 2–3 once bene esse is allowed its usual light hiatus or partial elision. Col10–12's repeated hexameter strings still force multiple defective feet (especially the anapaest in foot 2 and the irregular third/fourth feet) that the senarius frame avoids cleanly; their unelided 15-syllable forms only compound the problem by requiring extra position lengthening at quom and sit that the word boundaries do not support. Treating the fifth foot as SSL would demand exactly the same boundary inconsistency already rejected in feet 2–4, whereas the SLS reading keeps every secure long (et, nes, quom, sit, so, ma) and every observed open short intact. Further testing of the LSL trial in foot 5 would be useful only if it can be shown to preserve the same word-break tolerance without reintroducing the hexameter defects.
public_text.9: C1/C7/C14's LSS SL SL LL SLS SS framework continues to hold up well against the hexameter proposals, especially in preserving the observed shorts on bene, se, li, si and the second bi while respecting the word-break after soli quom.
